office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: New Albany-Floyd County Consolidated School Corporation (NAFCS) serves all of Floyd County, with headquarters in New Albany; it operates two high schools (Floyd Central and New Albany), three middle schools, nine elementary schools, an early learning center and the Prosser Career Center [24]. A current total enrollment figure was not found in fetched sources.

Superintendent Travis Madison, hired in 2023, left Sept. 25, 2026 for a post at Vincennes University [25, 26]. On Sept. 21, 2026 the board unanimously named former Crawford County and North Harrison superintendent Mark Eastridge interim superintendent; board President Rebecca Gardenour said she wants to begin the permanent search in January, after the November election [27]. (WDRB's report lists his prior district as South Harrison [28].)

The board has seven members serving four-year terms [29, 30]: Becky Gardenour (president, District 4), Thad Neafus (vice president, at large), Connie Baugh (secretary, at large), Ann Carruthers (at large), Elizabeth Galligan (District 3), Melanie Stumler Northup (District 1) and Lee Ann Wiseheart (District 2) [29, 30]. District members must live in their district, but voters across the county vote in every seat's race, according to SoINformed [31].

Four seats are on the 2026 ballot: District 1, District 2 and two at-large seats [32, 31]. The state list shows the at-large race as 'vote for 1', but the News and Tribune and SoINformed both describe two at-large seats [32, 31]; the two current at-large members whose terms end in 2026 (Baugh and Neafus) are both running [30, 32], and the 2022 at-large race was 'Vote For 2' [33]. Voters should check their ballot for the number to choose.

All four incumbents filed: Northup is unopposed in District 1, Wiseheart faces Steve Morris in District 2, and Baugh and Neafus face Brad Striegel and Heather Naville-Cooley for the two at-large seats [32, 34]. Of the seven candidates, Baugh and Neafus filed as Republicans and Morris as an Independent; the rest are nonpartisan [34, 35]. 2026 is the first Indiana election in which school board candidates could declare a party [32].

Budget and SEA 1 (Sept. 21, 2026): the CFO presented a draft 2027 budget of $165.7 million, to be adopted Oct. 19; he said the district lost more money than expected from the 2025 property-tax law (Senate Enrolled Act 1), projected a total loss of more than $5 million from it (more than $3 million from the operations fund), and said the budget is still on track to balance [36].

Facilities: under the Vision 2030 plan approved in December 2025, NAFCS may borrow up to $395 million for facility work [37, 26]. Proposals presented in June 2026 included two student activity centers estimated at $20 million each and $7 million in science-lab renovations at New Albany High [37]; 2027 capital plans include roof and HVAC work and two new elementary schools to replace Grant Line and Georgetown elementaries [36].

Public comment policy (Feb.–April 2026): after some residents used meetings to raise claims about district personnel, the board considered requiring advance approval for non-agenda comments; after tabling it twice, the board voted unanimously April 13 to keep the existing policy, amended so a set statement is read when a speaker is stopped [38, 39, 40].

Academic programs (2026): in May, eight speakers objected to a plan to phase out Latin at both high schools [41]; in August, the district first planned to replace middle-school Algebra I and Geometry for high-ability students with 'Advanced Math', then reversed course after parent objections, and Madison apologized for how the change was communicated [42, 43]. On June 8, 2026 the board unanimously approved a device policy to carry out the state's bell-to-bell student phone ban and reinstated the NAFCS Virtual Academy for 2026-27 [44].
Test scores: 91% of NAFCS third graders passed IREAD in 2026 [45]; in 2025, NAFCS had the highest ILEARN proficiency in the Clark-Floyd area (50.2% in English, 50.3% in math) [46].

Forums: a Sept. 10, 2026 meet-the-candidates open house hosted by Hoosier Action's TAG chapter drew five of the seven candidates (Neafus, Northup, Naville-Cooley, Morris and Striegel) [31]. SoINformed published a Floyd County voter guide questionnaire on Oct. 2, 2026 [47], but its candidate answers are in a separate Canva document that could not be read for this profile.

candidates.summary: Incumbent, unopposed; on the board since January 2023 [30, 32].
background: Mortgage loan officer since 2016 and owner of Greet Floyds Knobs magazine, according to her district board biography [30].
Served one year as board vice president and is the board's representative on the Floyd County Redevelopment Commission [30].
path_to_ballot: First elected to the District 1 seat in November 2022, succeeding Donna Corbett [48].

items: At the Sept. 10, 2026 open house, said building leaders should "support every program, whether you're an athlete, or a theater kid, or a band kid, or an orchestra kid" and that all students should get the same opportunities, as reported by SoINformed [31].
After her 2022 election, said her long-term hope was "to create a higher level of cohesiveness between the board and the community and the parents and administration" [48].

on_incumbent: Is a current board member [30]. No 2026 account by her of specific board votes was found in fetched sources.
endorsements_finance: No campaign finance report or endorsement for 2026 was found in fetched sources.
gaps: Her 2026 responses to the SoINformed questionnaire, if any, could not be read.
No 2026 statements on the budget, SEA 1, the superintendent search or the high-ability math change were found.

candidates.summary: Incumbent seeking a fifth term; on the board 2006-2010 and since 2014 [32, 49].
background: Listed by the district as a Floyd County adult probation officer and adult sex offender probation officer [30]; in 2022 the News and Tribune described her as a victim assistance coordinator for Jefferson County [49].
Founded K.I.P.S. in 2012, co-founded S.U.R.F. Board in 2006 and has more than 25 years of coaching experience, according to her board biography [30].
Has served in leadership with the Indiana School Boards Association [50].
path_to_ballot: Re-elected to District 2 in 2022 over two challengers [48].

items: At the April 13, 2026 meeting, urged strict adherence to the three-minute public-comment limit: "The policy won't mean squat if we don't abide by what the policy says" [40].
When a $20 million student activity center for New Albany High was proposed in June 2026, said the idea was "a lot" for her and asked why it was needed [37].
In 2022 named school safety a top priority and said she wanted to "stabilize" mental-health resources in schools [49].
In 2022 said she would build "a stable budget with responsible spending" and advocate for better teacher pay and benefits [49].

on_incumbent: Is a current board member [30]. Seconded the April 2026 motion to keep the public comment policy with an added statement [40].
endorsements_finance: No campaign finance report or endorsement for 2026 was found in fetched sources.
gaps: Did not attend the Sept. 10, 2026 open house, per SoINformed's list of attendees; no 2026 campaign statements found.
Her current occupation differs between her district bio and 2022 news coverage; not resolved.

candidates.summary: Challenger, listed as Independent; former superintendent of Lanesville Community School Corporation [32, 6].
background: Was superintendent of Lanesville Community School Corporation for 13 years, according to the News and Tribune [32].

items: At the Sept. 10, 2026 open house, said "Public education does so much for our community" and described defending public education as his reason for running, per SoINformed [31].

endorsements_finance: No campaign finance report or endorsement for 2026 was found in fetched sources.
gaps: No candidate website, social media page or detailed platform found.
Dates of his Lanesville tenure and his current occupation were not found.
No statements on the budget, SEA 1, facilities or the superintendent search found.

candidates.summary: Challenger; small business owner and former Floyd County Council member [32, 31].
background: Owner of C-TEK Security Systems, a home security company; served 12 years in the Floyd County Sheriff's Office reserve and 16 years on the Floyd County Council as a Democrat, per the News and Tribune [32].
Graduate of Indiana University and the Indiana Law Enforcement Academy, per a 2024 LPM voter guide [51].

items: At the Sept. 10, 2026 open house, said "Status quo - I'm not happy with that" and cited his government and business experience as preparation for funding challenges, per SoINformed [31].

on_incumbent: Said he is not happy with the "status quo" [31]; no more specific comment on board decisions was found.
endorsements_finance: No campaign finance report or endorsement for 2026 was found in fetched sources.
gaps: No candidate website or detailed platform found.
No statements on specific board decisions (Vision 2030, high-ability math, superintendent search) found.

candidates.summary: Incumbent seeking a second term; board secretary; listed as Republican [30, 32, 6].
background: A Floyd Central graduate whose children and grandchildren have attended NAFCS schools, per 2022 News and Tribune coverage [52].
Her district board biography lists no occupation [30].
path_to_ballot: Elected to an at-large seat in November 2022 [48].

items: In 2022 said parents should "have their voices back again" and that the board should be open to "fully answering the questions that the public and the parents are asking" [52].
In 2022 said she wanted more emphasis on civics and agriculture, and a return to "classical and traditional ways of teaching" [52, 48].

on_incumbent: Is a current board member and the board's secretary [29]. No 2026 account by her of the board's record was found in fetched sources.
endorsements_finance: In 2022, a political action committee called Liberty Defense endorsed her and sent mailers, per the News and Tribune [48].
No campaign finance report or endorsement for 2026 was found in fetched sources.
gaps: Did not attend the Sept. 10, 2026 open house, per SoINformed's attendee list; declined a News and Tribune interview in 2022.
No 2026 campaign statements found; positions above date from 2022.

candidates.summary: Challenger; chief operating officer of a New Albany trucking company [32].
background: Chief operating officer of All Star Trucking in New Albany, according to her LinkedIn profile as cited by the News and Tribune [32].
path_to_ballot: Filed June 15, 2026; listed without party (nonpartisan) [34, 6]. Her name appears as 'Heather Naville- Cooley' on official lists and 'Heather Naville-Cooley' in news coverage [34, 32].

items: At the Sept. 10, 2026 open house, said "The school system is really the driver for our economy" and argued that weak schools would drive residents and workers away, per SoINformed [31].

endorsements_finance: No campaign finance report or endorsement for 2026 was found in fetched sources.
gaps: No candidate website or detailed platform found.
No statements on the budget, facilities, or board decisions found.

candidates.summary: Incumbent seeking a second term; board vice president; listed as Republican [29, 32, 6].
background: Has worked for the Floyd County Sheriff's Department (nearly 28 years as of 2022, when he was a sergeant); a New Albany High graduate whose children attended NAFCS, per 2022 coverage [52, 50].
path_to_ballot: Filed May 26, 2026 as a Republican [34, 6]. He originally filed as a nonpartisan; he told the News and Tribune that public figures privately encouraged him to file as a Republican, and declined to say who [32].
Elected to an at-large seat in November 2022 [48].

items: At the Sept. 10, 2026 open house, pointed to upcoming challenges tied to "SB 1" and budget issues, per SoINformed [31].
In April 2026, said he would back keeping the public comment policy if it were amended to require a set statement when a speaker goes over time or is stopped [40].
In 2022 called for curriculum to be posted online so parents could see it [52].
In 2022 listed school safety, including school resource officers in all schools, as a priority [52].
In 2022 said he wanted to focus on reading, writing and arithmetic, and raised concerns about social-emotional learning and sex education [52].

on_incumbent: Is a current board member and vice president [29]. Cites his police experience working with diverse groups [31].
endorsements_finance: In 2022, a political action committee called Liberty Defense endorsed him and sent mailers, per the News and Tribune [48].
No campaign finance report or endorsement for 2026 was found in fetched sources.
gaps: Most of his detailed positions date from 2022; few 2026 statements found.
His current rank and role with the sheriff's department were not confirmed for 2026.
